records.topic: The Strait Carrying 400 Ships a Day
records.coreQuestion: How do more than 400 ships a day cross paths in the narrow Strait of Dover without colliding?
records.openingLine: Why 400 ships a day never collide here.
records.secondBeat: The Strait of Dover runs on strict one-way lanes.
records.dependency: North Sea ports and Atlantic trade depend on safe passage through the Strait of Dover.
records.mechanism: A strict scheme of one-way shipping lanes, watched around the clock from both coasts, separates opposing traffic.
records.bottleneck: Through-traffic crosses busy ferry routes between England and France in a narrow strait.
records.failureConsequence: A collision or grounding would block lanes used by hundreds of ships a day.
records.resilience: The Channel Tunnel carries some freight beneath the strait, but not deep-sea cargo.
records.expectedConsequence: ships queue and reroute while lanes are cleared
visualScenes: traffic separation lanes in the Strait of Dover
editorialTitles: The Busiest Strait Most People Never Think About
How 400 Ships a Day Share the Dover Strait

facts.claim: The strait is one of the busiest international seaways in the world, used by over 400 commercial vessels daily.
HM Coastguard and the Maritime Gendarmerie maintain a 24-hour watch over the strait and enforce a strict regime of shipping lanes.
The Channel Tunnel provides an alternative route, crossing beneath the strait at an average depth of 45 m (148 ft) below the seabed.
The first flood that formed the strait was about 425,000 years ago, when an ice-dammed lake in the southern North Sea overflowed.

narration.text: Why 400 ships a day never collide here.
The Strait of Dover runs on strict one-way lanes.
It's one of the busiest seaways in the world.
British and French coastguards watch it 24 hours a day.
Ferries between England and France must cut across the flow.
The Channel Tunnel runs 45 metres below the seabed, but carries no ships.
One collision here could stall traffic for North Sea ports.
That's why a painted-on-the-chart rulebook keeps trade moving.

records.topic: The Structure Stopping the Mississippi From Moving
records.coreQuestion: What keeps the Mississippi River from abandoning New Orleans for a shorter route to the sea?
records.openingLine: Why the Mississippi is held to 30% diversion.
records.secondBeat: Left alone, the river would shift to the Atchafalaya.
records.dependency: New Orleans, Baton Rouge and the river's industrial corridor depend on the Mississippi staying in its channel.
records.mechanism: Control gates at Old River cap how much of the Mississippi's flow can divert into the Atchafalaya River.
records.bottleneck: The river naturally wants to shift to the steeper Atchafalaya route; one structure holds it back.
records.failureConsequence: A failure would let the Mississippi change course, leaving ports on a stagnant channel.
records.resilience: An auxiliary structure was added after the 1973 flood nearly caused failure.
records.expectedConsequence: a river avulsion would reroute shipping, water supply and industry
visualScenes: map of the Mississippi and Atchafalaya split
editorialTitles: The Gate Holding the Mississippi in Place
Why the Mississippi Wants to Move

facts.claim: Between 1850 and 1950, the percentage of latitude flow entering the Atchafalaya River had increased from less than 10 percent to about 30 percent.
The Corps completed construction on the ORCS in 1963 to prevent the main channel flow of the Mississippi from altering its current course through avulsion.
The Mississippi flood of 1973 almost caused the control structure to fail.
By 1880, it rarely flowed eastward and was rapidly capturing more of the flow of the Mississippi.

narration.text: Why the Mississippi is held to 30% diversion.
Left alone, the river would shift to the Atchafalaya.
Between 1850 and 1950, that branch grew from under 10 to 30 percent.
In 1963, engineers finished the Old River Control Structure to stop it.
The 1973 flood almost made it fail.
Ports and refineries downstream depend on the river staying put.
If the river moved, they'd sit beside a fading channel.
That's why one set of gates holds back a whole river.

records.topic: The Twin Ports That Unload America's Imports
records.coreQuestion: Why does so much of America's imported cargo arrive through two neighbouring ports?
records.openingLine: Why America's busiest container port has a twin.
records.secondBeat: Los Angeles sits right beside the Port of Long Beach.
records.dependency: Retailers and manufacturers across the U.S. depend on cargo arriving at Los Angeles and Long Beach.
records.mechanism: Container terminals hand boxes to on-dock rail and trucks that carry them inland.
records.bottleneck: Terminal space, cranes and rail links concentrate transpacific imports into one bay.
records.failureConsequence: Congestion at the twin ports delays goods nationwide.
records.resilience: Other West Coast, Gulf and East Coast ports can take some diverted ships.
records.expectedConsequence: ships wait offshore and inland deliveries slip
visualScenes: aerial view of San Pedro Bay ports
editorialTitles: The Two Ports Behind America's Imports
Why Los Angeles and Long Beach Matter So Much

facts.claim: The port has 25 cargo terminals, 82 container cranes, eight container terminals, and 113 miles (182 km) of on-dock rail.
It occupies 7,500 acres of land and water with 43 miles (69 km) of waterfront and adjoins the separate Port of Long Beach.
The port is the busiest port in the United States by container volume, and the 10th-busiest worldwide when combined with the neighboring Port of Long Beach.
In 1985, the port handled one million containers in a year for the first time.

narration.text: Why America's busiest container port has a twin.
Los Angeles sits right beside the Port of Long Beach.
Los Angeles alone has 82 container cranes and 25 cargo terminals.
It adds 113 miles of on-dock rail.
Combined, the twin ports rank 10th in the world.
Transpacific cargo funnels into this single bay.
When it jams, store shelves far inland feel it.
That's why one bay can set the pace for a whole country's imports.

records.topic: The Airport Where Packages Change Planes at Night
records.coreQuestion: Why does so much overnight air freight fly through Memphis?
records.openingLine: Why 1 city sorts a million packages nightly.
records.secondBeat: FedEx built its main hub there in 1973.
records.dependency: Overnight parcel delivery across the U.S. depends on a central sorting hub where planes swap packages.
records.mechanism: Planes converge on one hub at night, packages are sorted, and flights depart before dawn.
records.bottleneck: A hub-and-spoke network concentrates the whole night's sort in one place.
records.failureConsequence: Weather or an outage at the hub delays packages across the network.
records.resilience: Regional hubs and ground networks absorb part of the volume.
records.expectedConsequence: next-day deliveries slip across the country
visualScenes: cargo jets lined up at night
editorialTitles: The Night Hub Behind Overnight Delivery
Why Memphis Became a Cargo Giant

facts.claim: In 1973, Federal Express established its main hub at the airport.
Memphis became the busiest airport by cargo traffic worldwide in 1992.
By 2000, the hub processed over one million packages per night, and FedEx ran 150 daily flights from Memphis.
As of 2018, Memphis was the second-busiest cargo airport in the world.
The airport opened the first air-cargo terminal in the country in February 1958.

narration.text: Why 1 city sorts a million packages nightly.
FedEx built its main hub there in 1973.
By 1992, it was the world's busiest cargo airport.
By 2000, FedEx ran 150 daily flights from the hub.
Planes fly in, packages swap planes, and flights leave before dawn.
One stormy night at the hub delays deliveries nationwide.
As of 2018, it was still the second-busiest cargo airport.
That's why overnight delivery depends on one city's night shift.

records.topic: The Power Lines Carrying Electricity 3,000 Kilometres
records.coreQuestion: How do grids move power thousands of kilometres, and why are the converters so critical?
records.openingLine: Why one Chinese power line runs 3,000 kilometres.
records.secondBeat: It uses direct current at 1,100 kilovolts.
records.dependency: Long-distance transmission, undersea interconnectors and offshore wind depend on HVDC converter stations.
records.mechanism: Converter valves turn alternating current into direct current for transmission, then back again.
records.bottleneck: Each link depends on custom converter stations at both ends.
records.failureConsequence: A converter outage removes the whole link's capacity at once.
records.resilience: Parallel AC lines and spare capacity elsewhere cover some of the loss.
records.expectedConsequence: grid operators lose a large block of imported power instantly
visualScenes: HVDC converter hall with valve towers
editorialTitles: The Converters Behind Long-Distance Power
Why HVDC Links Hinge on Their Converters

facts.claim: A high-voltage direct current (HVDC) system uses direct current and high voltages (currently between 100 kV and 800 kV) for electric power transmission.
The longest HVDC link in the world is the Zhundong–South Anhui link in China, a ±1,100 kV, ultra HVDC line with a length of more than 3,000 km (1,900 mi).
Early commercial installations included a 100 kV, 20 MW system between Gotland and mainland Sweden in 1954.
Other Thury systems operating at up to 100 kV DC worked into the 1930s, but the rotating machinery required high maintenance and had high energy loss.

narration.text: Why one Chinese power line runs 3,000 kilometres.
It uses direct current at 1,100 kilovolts.
Most HVDC links run between 100 and 800 kilovolts.
An early one linked Gotland to Sweden in 1954, at just 20 megawatts.
Converter stations at each end turn AC into DC and back.
Lose a converter, and the whole link's power drops at once.
That's why long-distance power depends on its two endpoints.

records.topic: The Small Generators That Restart a Dead Grid
records.coreQuestion: After a total blackout, how does a grid restart when power plants need power to start?
records.openingLine: Why big power plants can't restart themselves.
records.secondBeat: Steam plants use up to 10% of output just running.
records.dependency: Grid recovery after a blackout depends on units that can start without external power.
records.mechanism: Black-start units energise lines step by step so larger plants can restart.
records.bottleneck: Big steam plants need external power just to run their own pumps and fans.
records.failureConsequence: Without enough black-start capacity, restoring a grid takes far longer.
records.resilience: Batteries and grid-forming wind farms are now proving they can black-start too.
records.expectedConsequence: outages last longer when black-start units are scarce
visualScenes: dark city skyline during a blackout
editorialTitles: How a Dead Power Grid Comes Back
Why Power Plants Need Power to Start

facts.claim: A typical BS generator is a small (10–50 MW) hydro or gas turbine generation unit.
Generating plants using steam turbines require station service power of up to 10% of their capacity for boiler feedwater pumps, boiler forced-draft combustion air blowers, and for fuel preparation.
The first black start on Germany's grid was tested in 2017 at WEMAG battery power station in Schwerin on a disconnected, isolated grid.
In 2020, the 69 MW Dersalloch wind farm black-started part of the Scotland grid, using virtual synchronous machines.

narration.text: Why big power plants can't restart themselves.
Steam plants use up to 10% of output just running.
After a blackout, that power has to come from somewhere.
Small black-start units, often 10 to 50 megawatts, go first.
They energise lines step by step until bigger plants wake up.
In 2020, a 69-megawatt Scottish wind farm black-started part of the grid.
Without enough of these units, restoration drags on.
That's why a grid's restart button is its smallest generators.

records.topic: The Frankfurt Hub Moving 19.6 Terabits a Second
records.coreQuestion: Why does so much internet traffic meet in a few buildings in Frankfurt?
records.openingLine: Why 19.6 terabits a second meet in Frankfurt.
records.secondBeat: That's the peak throughput of DE-CIX, one exchange point.
records.dependency: Networks from more than 100 countries exchange traffic directly at DE-CIX in Frankfurt.
records.mechanism: Carriers, ISPs and content networks connect to a shared switching fabric and swap traffic without paying transit.
records.bottleneck: Peering concentrates huge volumes of traffic in a handful of data centres.
records.failureConsequence: An outage forces traffic onto longer, costlier transit routes, adding latency.
records.resilience: Networks usually keep backup transit links and other exchanges.
editorialTitles: Where the Internet's Networks Meet
Why Frankfurt Is an Internet Crossroads

facts.claim: The DE-CIX Internet exchange point situated in Frankfurt, Germany, is one of the largest IXPs worldwide, with throughput of 19.6 terabits per second (Tbit/s) in July 2026.
DE-CIX is accessible from data centers in over 600 cities worldwide and connects network operators from more than 100 countries.
The optical backbone has a total capacity of 48 terabits per second across a mesh-network topology.
DE-CIX has attracted networks from all over the world, leading to an annual traffic growth rate of up to 100 percent per year.

narration.text: Why 19.6 terabits a second meet in Frankfurt.
That's the peak throughput of DE-CIX, one exchange point.
It links networks from more than 100 countries.
They swap traffic directly, instead of paying others to carry it.
Its optical backbone can carry 48 terabits per second.
If it fails, traffic detours over longer, pricier routes.
That's why the internet's shortcuts run through a few buildings.

records.topic: The Signal Every Plane Broadcasts Once a Second
records.coreQuestion: How do controllers see aircraft where radar can't reach?
records.openingLine: Why planes broadcast their position every second.
records.dependency: Air traffic control in many regions depends on aircraft broadcasting their own GPS positions.
records.mechanism: Aircraft broadcast position reports every second on 1090 MHz or 978 MHz, picked up by ground stations and other aircraft.
records.bottleneck: The system trusts satellite navigation on board each aircraft.
records.failureConsequence: If GPS is jammed or a transmitter fails, the aircraft drops out of the shared picture.
records.resilience: Radar and procedural separation remain as backups in many areas.
records.expectedConsequence: controllers widen spacing when position data drops
visualScenes: air traffic control screen with aircraft icons
GPS satellite to aircraft to ground station diagram
editorialTitles: The Signal That Replaced Radar in Remote Skies
How Planes Announce Themselves Every Second

facts.claim: The most common ADS-B data links operate at 1090 MHz, essentially a modified Mode S transponder, or at 978 MHz.
In both forms of ADS-B (1090ES & 978 MHz UAT), the position report is updated once per second.
Canada uses ADS-B for surveillance in remote regions not covered by traditional radar since 15 January 2009.
Since implementation of the FAA's ADS-B Out equipage requirement on January 1, 2020, ADS-B has become the FAA's preferred surveillance technology.
The FAA would like aircraft that operate exclusively below 18,000 feet to use the 978 MHz link, to alleviate congestion of the 1090 MHz frequency.

narration.text: Why planes broadcast their position every second.
That's ADS-B, on 1090 or 978 megahertz.
Canada has used it since 2009 where radar can't reach.
The FAA required it from January 1, 2020.
Aircraft below 18,000 feet are steered to 978 MHz to ease congestion.
Each report depends on the plane's own satellite navigation.
Jam that signal, and aircraft fade from the shared picture.
That's why modern air traffic control trusts planes to report themselves.

records.topic: The Baggage System That Delayed an Entire Airport
records.coreQuestion: How did an automated baggage system help delay a new airport's opening, and why was it scrapped?
records.openingLine: Why Denver's airport opening kept slipping.
records.secondBeat: Its automated baggage system was a condition of the deal.
records.dependency: Airports depend on baggage systems to move luggage between check-in, aircraft and reclaim on tight connections.
records.mechanism: Conveyors and carts route each bag through tunnels to the right aircraft or carousel.
records.bottleneck: A single integrated system must work for every airline and every flight at once.
records.failureConsequence: When it jams, flights leave without bags or wait for them.
records.resilience: Manual handling can replace automation, at higher labour cost.
records.expectedConsequence: connections are missed and bags pile up
visualScenes: opening date slipping on a calendar
bags piling up at a jam
editorialTitles: The Baggage System That Delayed an Airport
Why Denver Gave Up on Its Robot Luggage Carts

facts.claim: The airline finally relented under the condition that the airport include an automated baggage system.
Construction delays pushed opening day back, first to December 1993, then to March 1994.
In April 1994, the city invited reporters to observe the first test of the new automated baggage system.
The baggage system continued to be a maintenance hassle and was finally terminated in September 2005, with traditional baggage handlers manually handling cargo and passenger luggage.
The actual use for the tunnels is to move luggage between check-in counters, airplanes and baggage claim areas.

narration.text: Why Denver's airport opening kept slipping.
Its automated baggage system was a condition of the deal.
Tunnels move luggage between check-in, planes and baggage claim.
Opening day slid to December 1993, then March 1994.
In April 1994, reporters watched the system's first test.
It stayed a maintenance hassle until it was scrapped in 2005.
Humans went back to handling the bags.
That's why the humble bag belt can decide when an airport opens.

records.topic: The 2,300-Tonne Engine Driving a Container Ship
records.coreQuestion: What does it take to push a giant container ship across an ocean?
records.openingLine: Why one 2,300-tonne engine drives a whole ship.
records.dependency: Large container ships depend on a single slow-speed diesel engine turning one propeller.
records.mechanism: A two-stroke engine turns the propeller shaft directly, without a gearbox.
records.bottleneck: One engine per ship means no redundancy for propulsion.
records.failureConsequence: An engine failure leaves a ship drifting until tugs or repairs arrive.
records.resilience: Crews carry spare parts and can repair many faults at sea.
records.expectedConsequence: a disabled ship drifts and can block traffic
visualScenes: engine as tall as a four-storey building
power comparison with a power plant
editorialTitles: The Giant Engine Inside a Container Ship
Why One Engine Moves a Whole Ship

facts.claim: Its largest 14-cylinder version is 13.5 m (44 ft) high, 26.59 m (87.2 ft) long, weighs over 2,300 t, and produces 80.08 MW (107,390 hp).
The 14-cylinder version first entered commercial service in September 2006 aboard the Emma Mærsk.
The Wärtsilä RT-flex96C is a two-stroke turbocharged low-speed diesel engine designed by WinGD.
As of 2006, more than 300 RT-flex96C engines and older RTA96C engines were in service or on order.

narration.text: Why one 2,300-tonne engine drives a whole ship.
The largest version produces 80 megawatts.
It stands 13.5 metres high and 26.59 metres long.
It first went to sea in 2006 aboard the Emma Mærsk.
It's a slow two-stroke diesel, turning the propeller directly.
Most big ships carry just one main engine.
If it stops, the ship drifts until help arrives.
That's why a single machine decides whether cargo keeps moving.

records.topic: The Rail Yard Sorting 3,000 Cars a Day
records.coreQuestion: How does the world's largest rail yard sort thousands of freight cars every day?
records.openingLine: Why 14,000 rail cars pass one yard daily.
records.secondBeat: Bailey Yard in Nebraska sorts about 3,000 of them.
records.dependency: U.S. freight trains depend on hump yards to break up and rebuild trains by destination.
records.mechanism: Cars are pushed over a hump and roll by gravity into the right track.
records.bottleneck: Huge volumes of cars funnel through a few big sorting yards.
records.failureConsequence: A yard slowdown ripples delays across the rail network.
records.resilience: Railroads reroute trains or sort at other yards at lower capacity.
records.expectedConsequence: shipments wait as cars back up at the yard
visualScenes: freight car rolling over the hump
editorialTitles: The Giant Rail Yard That Sorts America's Freight
How Gravity Sorts 3,000 Freight Cars a Day

facts.claim: An average of 139 trains and over 14,000 railroad cars pass through Bailey Yard every day.
The yard sorts approximately 3,000 cars daily using the yard's two humps.
Bailey Yard has 200 separate tracks totaling 315 miles (507 km) of track, 985 switches, 766 turnouts, and 17 receiving and 16 departure tracks.
The humps sort four cars per minute into one of the 114 bowl tracks.
The eastbound hump is a 34 foot (10 m) tall mound, and the westbound hump is 20 feet (6.1 m) high.

narration.text: Why 14,000 rail cars pass one yard daily.
Bailey Yard in Nebraska sorts about 3,000 of them.
It handles an average of 139 trains a day.
Cars roll over a 34-foot hump and sort by gravity.
That's 4 cars a minute into 114 bowl tracks.
The yard spans 315 miles of track.
A slowdown here delays freight across the network.
That's why a hill of dirt still sorts America's freight.

records.topic: Why 2 mm of Rain Sent Sewage Into the Thames
records.coreQuestion: Why did London's Victorian sewers overflow into the Thames after light rain?
records.openingLine: Why 2 mm of rain fouled the Thames.
records.secondBeat: London's Victorian sewers carry rain and sewage together.
records.dependency: London's sewer network carries both rainwater and sewage in the same pipes.
records.mechanism: When pipes fill, combined sewer overflows release the excess into the river instead of homes.
records.bottleneck: A system designed for a smaller city now serves a far denser one.
records.failureConsequence: Overflows discharge raw sewage into the river, sometimes weekly.
records.resilience: The Thames Tideway Tunnel intercepts overflows and carries them to treatment.
records.expectedConsequence: river pollution rises with each heavy rain
visualScenes: combined sewer overflow outfall on the Thames
editorialTitles: Why London's Sewers Spill Into the Thames
The Super Sewer Built for 2 mm of Rain

facts.claim: Bazalgette's system had the ability to overflow into the Thames via 57 combined sewer overflows (CSOs) along the banks of the river.
By 2011 overflows into the river took place more than once a week and as little as 2 mm of rainfall could trigger a discharge.
In 2001, London's population density was 18,457 people per square kilometre, compared to just 6,825 per square kilometre in Bazalgette's day.
The 2021-22 annual report gave an updated cost of £4.3bn.
The first sewage flowed into the tunnel in September 2024.

narration.text: Why 2 mm of rain fouled the Thames.
London's Victorian sewers carry rain and sewage together.
When full, they spill through 57 overflows into the river.
Density more than doubled, from 6,825 to 18,457 people per square kilometre.
By 2011, overflows happened more than once a week.
A £4.3 billion super sewer now intercepts them.
The first sewage flowed into it in September 2024.
That's why a city's river quality hinges on its oldest pipes.

records.topic: The System Settling $15.4 Trillion in a Day
records.coreQuestion: How does the currency market avoid one bank paying and never getting paid back?
records.openingLine: Why $15.4 trillion once settled in a day.
records.secondBeat: CLS settles both sides of a currency trade together.
records.dependency: Much of the global foreign exchange market settles through CLS to remove settlement risk.
records.mechanism: Payment-versus-payment settlement releases both legs of a currency trade together or not at all.
records.bottleneck: A single system settles a large share of the world's currency trades.
records.failureConsequence: Without it, banks face the risk that a counterparty fails mid-settlement, as in 1974.
records.resilience: Banks can settle bilaterally, but with more risk and more liquidity needed.
records.expectedConsequence: settlement risk and liquidity demands would rise sharply
visualScenes: currency trade with two payment legs
editorialTitles: The System That Settles the Currency Market
Why a 1974 Bank Collapse Still Shapes FX

facts.claim: Settlement risk is known as Herstatt Risk, after the German bank Bankhaus Herstatt, which collapsed in June 1974 leaving many of its FX counterparties with significant losses.
Since it began operations in 2002, CLS has rapidly increased and by March 2017 was settling just over 50% of global FX transactions.
The single day record for value settled is US$15.4 trillion, set on 15 December 2021.
The single day record for volume settled is 3.2 million trades, set on 5 July 2022.

narration.text: Why $15.4 trillion once settled in a day.
CLS settles both sides of a currency trade together.
By 2017, it handled just over 50% of global FX trades.
It exists because of Herstatt, a bank that collapsed in 1974.
Its partners paid in, but never got paid back.
Its busiest day by volume was 3.2 million trades.
That's why the currency market runs on one settlement system.

records.topic: The Day the Internet Ran Out of Addresses
records.coreQuestion: What happened when the internet's original address system ran out of numbers?
records.openingLine: Why the internet's 4.3 billion addresses ran out.
records.secondBeat: IPv4 was designed long before phones and smart devices.
records.dependency: Every device on the internet needs an address, originally from IPv4's fixed pool.
records.mechanism: IANA allocates address blocks to regional registries, which assign them to networks.
records.bottleneck: IPv4 was designed with fewer than 4.3 billion addresses.
records.failureConsequence: Once pools ran dry, networks had to share addresses or move to IPv6.
records.resilience: Address sharing and IPv6 extend capacity, but add complexity.
records.expectedConsequence: address markets and translation layers spread
visualScenes: IANA handing blocks to regional registries
editorialTitles: The Day the Internet Ran Out of Addresses
Why IPv4's 4.3 Billion Weren't Enough

facts.claim: Because the original Internet architecture had fewer than 4.3 billion addresses available, depletion had been anticipated since the late 1980s.
The top-level exhaustion occurred on 31 January 2011.
IANA proceeded to allocate one of the five remaining /8s to each RIR, exhausting the IANA pool, at a ceremony and press conference on 3 February 2011.
APNIC was the first regional Internet registry to run out of freely allocated IPv4 addresses, on 15 April 2011.
In early 2011, only 16–26% of computers were IPv6 capable, while only 0.2% preferred IPv6 addressing.

narration.text: Why the internet's 4.3 billion addresses ran out.
IPv4 was designed long before phones and smart devices.
The central pool hit its limit on 31 January 2011.
On 3 February 2011, the last blocks went to regional registries.
Asia's registry ran out first, on 15 April 2011.
Back then, only 16 to 26% of computers could use IPv6.
So networks began sharing addresses behind translators.
That's why a numbering standard still shapes how you connect.

records.coreQuestion: Why does modern machining depend on a metal mostly supplied by one country?
records.secondBeat: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element.
records.dependency: Cutting tools, drill bits and wear parts depend on tungsten carbide.
records.mechanism: Tungsten powder is heated with carbon to form carbide, then pressed and sintered into tools.
records.bottleneck: Mined supply is concentrated in China, far ahead of other producers.
records.failureConsequence: Export curbs would squeeze tool makers and heavy industry worldwide.
records.resilience: Recycled scrap supplies about a third of tungsten; other mines are small.
records.expectedConsequence: tool prices rise and lead times stretch
visualScenes: tungsten carbide drill bit cutting steel
production share bar China versus others
editorialTitles: The Metal Behind Every Cutting Tool
Why Tungsten Supply Is So Concentrated

facts.claim: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all known elements, at 3,422 °C (6,192 °F; 3,695 K).
About 50% of tungsten is used in tungsten carbide, with the remaining major use being alloys and steels.
In 2025, China, Vietnam and Kazakhstan were the leading suppliers with 67,000, 3,000 an 2,400 tonnes, respectively.
In 2013 about 34% of total tungsten production came from recycled tungsten-rich scrap, rather than from mined ores.
Tungsten carbides (W2C and WC) are produced by heating powdered tungsten with carbon.

narration.text: Why tool makers need 3,422 °C tungsten.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element.
About 50% of it becomes tungsten carbide for cutting tools.
In 2025, China supplied 67,000 tonnes.
The next supplier, Vietnam, supplied 3,000.
Recycled scrap provided about 34% of production in 2013.
Export limits would hit machine shops worldwide.
That's why the hardest tools rest on a narrow supply chain.

records.topic: The Rock Formation Holding 75% of the World's Platinum
records.coreQuestion: Why does most of the world's platinum come from one geological formation in South Africa?
records.openingLine: Why 75% of platinum sits in one formation.
records.secondBeat: It's South Africa's Bushveld Complex, as big as Ireland.
records.dependency: Catalytic converters, fuel cells and chemical catalysts depend on platinum-group metals.
records.mechanism: Thin ore reefs in the Bushveld Complex are mined deep underground and refined into platinum and palladium.
records.bottleneck: A single igneous complex holds most known platinum resources.
records.failureConsequence: Power cuts, strikes or mine closures in the region tighten global supply.
records.resilience: Recycling of catalytic converters and Russian palladium add supply.
records.expectedConsequence: prices spike when Bushveld output falls
visualScenes: thin Merensky Reef layer in rock
editorialTitles: The Rock That Holds the World's Platinum
Why Platinum Supply Hangs on One Formation

facts.claim: It represents about 75 percent of the world's platinum and about 50 percent of the world's palladium resources.
It covers over 66,000 km2 (25,000 sq mi), an area the size of Ireland.
The Merensky and UG2 reefs contain approximately 90% of the world's known PGM reserves.
About 80% of the platinum and 20% of the palladium mined each year are produced from these horizons.
The Reef contains an average of 10 ppm platinum group metals.

narration.text: Why 75% of platinum sits in one formation.
It's South Africa's Bushveld Complex, as big as Ireland.
It also holds about 50% of palladium resources.
Two thin reefs contain about 90% of known reserves.
They produce about 80% of the platinum mined each year.
Catalytic converters and fuel cells depend on that supply.
Power cuts or strikes there move prices worldwide.
That's why one ancient magma body shapes car exhaust rules.
